reference.source: Grabb & Smith's Plastic Surgery / standard references
clinicalPearls: Pressure ulcers arise over bony prominences (sacrum, ischium, greater trochanter, heel, occiput) where sustained pressure exceeds capillary perfusion pressure
Staging ranges from non-blanchable erythema of intact skin, through partial and full thickness skin loss, to exposure of muscle, tendon, or bone, with unstageable ulcers obscured by slough or eschar
The visible skin defect often underestimates the true extent, as necrosis is frequently more advanced in the deeper tissues nearest the bone
Prevention through repositioning, pressure-redistributing surfaces, skin care, moisture control, and nutrition is more effective than treatment of established ulcers
Management principles include pressure offloading, debridement of nonviable tissue, moist wound care, optimisation of nutrition, and control of spasticity, incontinence, and infection
Deep ulcers with dead space or exposed bone may require surgical debridement and reconstruction with local flaps, and osteomyelitis should be considered when bone is exposed
Flap reconstruction is offered to selected, optimised patients, and recurrence is common if the underlying causes of pressure and shear are not corrected
A multidisciplinary approach addressing mobility, sensation, continence, and social circumstances is essential to prevent recurrence
reference.pathophysiology: Pressure ulcers result from prolonged unrelieved pressure, often combined with shear and friction, that compresses soft tissue between bone and an external surface. When interface pressure exceeds capillary closing pressure, local ischaemia and impaired lymphatic drainage lead to tissue hypoxia, accumulation of metabolic waste, and cell death. Muscle is more susceptible to ischaemia than skin, so damage typically begins in deep tissue near the bony prominence and progresses outward, producing a cone-shaped area of necrosis. Contributing factors include immobility, impaired sensation, malnutrition, moisture, incontinence, vascular disease, and advanced age.
additionalDifferentials: Moisture-associated skin damage or incontinence dermatitis
Skin malignancy arising in a chronic wound (Marjolin ulcer)
Deep tissue infection or necrotising fasciitis
additionalInvestigations: Wound assessment with staging, measurement, and photographic documentation
Nutritional assessment including albumin and prealbumin
Wound or bone cultures and inflammatory markers when infection is suspected
Imaging (MRI or bone biopsy) to evaluate for underlying osteomyelitis
Assessment of vascular supply and tissue perfusion
Screening for and management of contributing factors such as spasticity and incontinence
redFlags: Spreading cellulitis, systemic sepsis, or signs of necrotising infection arising from the ulcer
Rapid deterioration or deep tissue injury under intact skin
Chronic non-healing ulcer with atypical features suggesting malignant transformation
reference.prognosis: Superficial pressure injuries can heal with conservative care once pressure is relieved, but deep ulcers heal slowly and often require surgery. Even after successful flap reconstruction, recurrence rates are high in patients who remain immobile or insensate, so long-term outcome depends heavily on ongoing prevention and management of underlying risk factors.
pitfalls: Underestimating the depth of tissue damage from the surface appearance alone
Attempting surgical closure without first correcting pressure, nutrition, spasticity, and incontinence
Failing to debride nonviable tissue and eschar before assessing wound bed
Overlooking underlying osteomyelitis in deep ulcers with exposed bone
Neglecting prevention and repositioning, leading to new or recurrent ulcers
Missing malignant change in a long-standing chronic ulcer
management: Relieve interface pressure with a structured repositioning schedule and pressure-redistributing support surfaces such as specialised mattresses and cushions
Debride nonviable tissue (sharp/surgical, enzymatic, or autolytic) to remove slough and eschar and expose a viable wound bed
Provide stage-appropriate moist wound care with dressings matched to exudate, depth, and dead space
Optimise nutrition with adequate protein and energy intake and correction of deficiencies to support healing
Control contributing factors including moisture and incontinence, spasticity, and skin protection
Treat wound infection with culture-directed antibiotics and evaluate for underlying osteomyelitis when bone is exposed
Refer deep ulcers with dead space or exposed bone for surgical debridement and reconstruction with local or myocutaneous flaps
Coordinate a tissue-viability, plastic surgery, and dietetic multidisciplinary team with ongoing prevention to reduce recurrence
